column4: The same root becomes direct sun exposure in وَلَا تَضْحَىٰ: Adam is promised freedom from thirst and the sun's heat, making explicit the heat latent in the section's forenoon.
وَٱلشَّمْسِ وَضُحَىٰهَا attributes ḍuḥā to the sun itself, directly joining the section's oath-word to solar light and heat.
After the night is darkened, وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَىٰهَا says that God brings out the earth's forenoon brightness; this is the same night-to-ḍuḥā emergence staged in surah 93.
The Garden guarantee begins with freedom from hunger and nakedness; together with 20:119 it binds adequate food to shelter from exposure, the same pairing the section hears in the forenoon.
This warning identifies the enemy who would expel Adam and his wife from the Garden and thereby expose Adam to hardship; 20:118-119 specify that hardship as hunger, thirst, nakedness, and sun.
Feeding on a day of severe hunger is the Quran's direct answer to the section's forenoon table standing against bad nourishment.
The first named recipient of that famine-day meal is a related orphan, directly joining the section's table to its command not to overpower the orphan.
This ayah adds the destitute person lying in dust to the orphan of 90:15, completing the concrete company at the hunger-day table.
عَيْلَةً is the same poverty root as the section's عَائِلًا, and يُغْنِيكُمُ ٱللَّهُ repeats the movement from feared poverty to God's enrichment found in 93:8.
Moses says آتِنَا غَدَآءَنَا, “bring our morning meal”; الغداء is precisely the source-section dictionary gloss used to disclose a meal inside ḍuḥā.

Hell's skins repeatedly become cooked through, نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُمْ; the source-section definition of qaly likewise says meat is roasted until it is made ناضج, so the dictionary cooking sense becomes a Quranic bodily scene.
Garments of fire and boiling liquid poured over heads begin the flesh-and-fire scene whose bodily effect 22:20 states, closely realizing the section's culinary senses of qaly and qahr as punishment.
Boiling liquid melts what is in bellies and the skins, directly corresponding to the source-section qahr image in which fire takes meat and its moisture runs out.
Those who consume an orphan's property are said to eat fire into their bellies; this single ayah fuses the section's orphan, eating, oppression, and fire images.
The sacrificial camels are eaten from and used to feed both the contented and the petitioner; this directly meets the source-section qaliyya made from camel meat and its table set against want.
People are told to eat from the sacrificial livestock and feed the afflicted poor, joining the source-section meat meal to relief of bad nourishment.
Abraham brings a roasted calf, عِجْلٍ حَنِيذٍ, a direct Quranic scene for the source-section qaly sense of cooking meat over heat until done.
God makes fire for people from the green tree, مِنَ ٱلشَّجَرِ ٱلْأَخْضَرِ نَارًا; this closely matches the source-section qily made by burning green plants.
The question about the fire people kindle places ordinary, deliberately kindled fire before the reader, the agent behind the section's frying and boiling senses.
This ayah asks whether people produced the fire's tree or God did, paralleling 36:80 and grounding the section's plant-to-fire image in divine provision.
The kindled fire is called a reminder and a provision for travelers, giving useful fire a food-and-sustenance setting rather than leaving it only as punishment.
لَبَنًا خَالِصًا, pure palatable milk, is the exact foodstuff from which the source-section qahīra is made before hot stones and flour are added.
One ayah places drinking what is in livestock's bellies beside eating from the animals; it gathers the milk base of qahīra and the meat base of qaliyya in a single provision scene.
Entering a fiercely hot fire begins a passage in which heat, boiling drink, and failed nourishment are made one punishment, reversing the section's warm morning table.
Drink from a boiling spring adds scalding liquid to the fire of 88:4 and the unnourishing food of 88:6-7.
The diners have no food except thorny growth, a concrete table of bad nourishment set within the passage's fire and boiling heat.
لَا يُسْمِنُ وَلَا يُغْنِى مِن جُوعٍ explicitly defines that food as neither nourishing nor relieving hunger, the clearest Quranic counterpart to the section's “bad nourishment.”
The righteous feed food, despite loving or needing it, to the poor person, orphan, and captive; this directly realizes the section's nourishing table for the vulnerable orphan.
The feeders of 76:8 are rewarded in the Garden where they see neither sun nor bitter cold, directly paralleling Adam's protection from sun exposure in 20:119.
Near shade and lowered fruit join shelter from the sun to readily available food, making visible both sides of the section's forenoon image.
The rebuke “you do not honor the orphan” supplies the social opposite of 93:9 and leads immediately to the failure to feed in 89:18.
Failure to urge one another to feed the poor directly opposes the forenoon table and completes the orphan-and-food pair begun in 89:17.
Harshly driving away the orphan is a concrete enactment of the qahr forbidden in 93:9 and is paired with refusal of poor feeding in the next ayah.
Not urging the feeding of the poor completes 107:2's orphan oppression with the bad nourishment heard by the section in the عيل family.
God “fed them against hunger” states in compact form the provision that the section's forenoon meal sets against malnutrition.
The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor; the same passage then replaces the withheld meal with the eater's own repellent food in 69:36-37.
The punishment offers no food except ghislīn, turning refusal to feed the poor in 69:34 into a corrupt punitive table.
Only the sinners eat that food, identifying the diners at the inverted table created by 69:34 and 69:36.
“We did not feed the poor” is one of the inhabitants' own reasons for reaching Saqar, directly binding withheld nourishment to the surah's fire imagery.
The disbelievers answer a command to spend by asking why they should feed someone God could feed; it is an explicit refusal of the provision-table the section makes visible.
Cloud shade and the descent of manna and quails place shelter from exposure and good food in one divine gift, the same conjunction made explicit in 20:118-119.
This parallel wilderness scene again combines cloud shade with manna and quails, then commands the people to eat the good things provided.
God provides shade, shelters, and garments that protect from heat, سَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ ٱلْحَرَّ, a direct answer to the sun exposure latent in ḍuḥā.
At the eastern limit the sun rises upon people for whom no screen from it was made; this is the Quran's most concrete scene of unshielded solar exposure.
The tree of zaqqum is introduced as food before its heat effect is described, beginning an inverted meal that culminates in boiling inside the eater.
Calling zaqqum “the food of the sinner” fixes the plant as a meal rather than generic fire imagery.
That food is like molten substance in the bellies, moving the cooking heat inside flesh in a way that echoes the section's qaly and qahr definitions.
It boils like boiling water, كَغَلْىِ ٱلْحَمِيمِ, directly matching the source-section qahīra's boiling-food scene while reversing nourishment into punishment.
The passage explicitly asks whether Garden hospitality or the tree of zaqqum is the better welcome, framing Hell's burning food as an anti-table.
The food-tree grows from the bottom of Hell, physically joining vegetation and fire as the source-section qily image does.
The condemned eat from the tree and fill their bellies, making its status as punitive nourishment concrete.
A mixture of boiling water follows the zaqqum meal, joining eating and scalding liquid as in the section's hot-food senses.
Eating from the tree of zaqqum begins another explicit punitive meal in a passage saturated with boiling heat.
Filling bellies from zaqqum specifies the bodily destination of the meal rather than invoking fire only in general.
Drinking boiling water after the food supplies the meal's searing liquid counterpart.
Drinking like desperately thirsty camels turns the source-section camel meal into a grim reversal in which camel thirst describes the diners.
Calling the sequence their “hospitality” on the Day of Judgment makes the whole passage a deliberate inversion of a nourishing table.
Hoarded metal is heated in Hell and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs, a direct Quranic instance of fire taking hold of bodily flesh.
Saqar is described as scorching the human skin, a concise bodily realization of the source-section qahr image of fire seizing meat.
The blaze is named as an inescapable fire before 70:16 specifies its action upon the body.
The blaze strips away the skin or extremities, directly showing fire overpowering flesh as in the source-section culinary qahr expression.
Pharaoh promises to kill sons and declares وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَٰهِرُونَ; this is the same qahr as human domination, exemplifying the cruelty excluded by the command concerning the orphan.
The garden owners swear to harvest early in the morning, beginning a morning food scene whose intended exclusion of the poor is stated in 68:24.
Their morning call to one another keeps the denial of food in a deliberately early-day setting, a dark counterpart to the forenoon meal.
They conspire that no poor person should enter the garden that day, directly opposing the section's meal set against deprivation.
When the garden is lost they confess that they themselves have been deprived, reversing their planned deprivation of the poor back upon them.

One ayah contrasts Garden rivers of milk whose taste never changes with boiling water that cuts intestines; it places the source-section qahīra's pure milk and boiling bodily harm on opposite sides of the final boundary.
God commands the intended burning fire to become coolness and safety for Abraham, the clearest reversal of the section's image of fire taking flesh.
Abraham's people propose killing or burning him, but God saves him from the fire in the same ayah; the fire-to-flesh action is explicitly attempted and excluded.
Those who refuse to march cite the heat, and the reply says Hell's fire is hotter; worldly solar heat and punitive fire are directly measured against each other.
وَلَا ٱلظِّلُّ وَلَا ٱلْحَرُورُ sets shade and scorching heat as non-equivalent opposites, clarifying the boundary between shelter and the exposure sensed in ḍuḥā.
The condemned are sent toward a three-branched “shade,” setting up a counterfeit shelter whose failure against flame is stated in 77:31.
That smoke is neither shading nor protective from the flame, reversing the genuine protection from heat in 16:81 and the Garden promise in 20:119.
Scorching wind and boiling water replace the gentle warmth and meal heard in the forenoon with lethal heat and drink.
The shadow is made of black smoke, converting the shelter associated with relief from sun into a product of fire.
The smoky shade is neither cool nor pleasant, expressly denying the two qualities a sheltering shade should give.
The inhabitants taste neither coolness nor drink, reversing both relief from heat and the thirst protection promised to Adam.
Only boiling water and foul fluid answer the absence of drink in 78:24, turning provision into burning harm.
The drink of the wrongdoers is like molten metal and scalds faces; a served drink becomes the agent of the section's fire-on-flesh image.
The same surah that defines the steep path through feeding an orphan and destitute person ends with fire closed over the rejecters, setting table and enclosing fire on opposite outcomes.
After rebuking failure to honor the orphan and feed the poor, the passage has Hell brought into view; neglected nourishment and fire thus meet as cause and consequence.
The deeply mindful person is kept away from the blaze, excluding fire from the giver whose defining act follows in 92:18.
Giving wealth for purification identifies the human act paired with escape from fire in 92:17, a thematic counterpart to feeding the vulnerable rather than subjecting them to want.
The people of the towns feel secure from punishment arriving ضُحًى while they play; the same forenoon that suggests warmth and a meal can also be the exposed hour of sudden judgment.
A lush, fruitful garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burned; it supplies the destructive reversal behind the source-section qily made by burning living plants.
God alone is ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ; divine mastery over all servants marks the boundary against a human being's forbidden qahr of an orphan.
Again naming God ٱلْقَاهِرُ above His servants in a context of guardianship and death distinguishes absolute divine qahr from human abuse of the unprotected.
Joseph contrasts scattered lords with Allah, ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ; in prison, the title locates ultimate domination in the one God rather than human masters.
After denying that powerless partners create as God creates, the ayah names Him ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ; this cosmic qahr sets a limit on the human domination forbidden in the section.
All creatures emerge before ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ on the transformed earth, making qahr universal divine sovereignty rather than license to crush a vulnerable person.
The messenger declares no deity but Allah, ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ; the divine title provides the theological boundary around the section's prohibition of human qahr.
In rejecting divine offspring, the ayah closes with ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ, assigning unconstrained qahr to God alone.
On the day all are exposed, sovereignty belongs to Allah, ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ; universal divine qahr contrasts with domination of an orphan in ordinary human life.
Moses fixes the contest for the festival day when people are gathered ضُحًى; it preserves the root's public forenoon-time sense alongside the heat and meal senses developed by the section.
The Last Hour will seem no longer than an evening or its ضُحى; the root here measures a day's brief span, adding transience to the section's warm forenoon.
The rising sun inclines away from the cave and the setting sun passes its occupants by, making their preservation partly a scene of controlled solar exposure.
God extends shade and makes the sun its indicator, showing sun and shade as a measured relation rather than treating forenoon heat in isolation.
God then draws the extended shade in gradually, making relief from sun a bestowed and measured condition.
The people of the Garden receive their provision morning and evening; the morning period thus carries a table in the Quran as the source dictionary says of ḍuḥā.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening; the recurring morning that can announce a meal becomes recurring exposure to flame.
“Purify your garments” meets the source-section qily definition at its stated use: an ash preparation with which clothes are washed.
The deeds of disbelievers are likened to ashes blown violently on a stormy day; the ayah supplies the ash that remains after the source-section qily plants are burned.
The command that a human being look at his food opens a provision sequence that includes the grain named in the source-section qaly definition.
God causes grain to grow from the split earth; grain is explicitly the other food the source-section says can be fried by qaly.
The revived earth brings out grain “from which they eat,” supplying both the qaly dictionary's grain object and its purpose as nourishment.
Feeding ten poor people must come from the average food one feeds one's own family, giving a concrete standard of adequate nourishment against the section's bad-feeding sense.
“Food that chokes” and painful punishment make the meal itself unfit and harmful, another specific Quranic reversal of nourishing provision.
The kindled fire of God identifies the agent whose penetration into the body is completed in 104:7.
The fire rises over the hearts, carrying the section's fire-taking-flesh image from the outer body to its interior.
Guardians are forbidden to consume orphan property wastefully; the rich must abstain and a poor guardian may take only fairly, setting a precise boundary where eating, poverty, and orphan care meet.
The prohibition on consuming an orphan's property into one's own wealth turns predatory “eating” into a form of the qahr the section forbids.
The demanded sign is a sacrificial offering consumed by fire, a direct meeting of food or flesh with the consuming fire disclosed by the section's qaly and qahr senses.
Abraham's opponents explicitly command one another to burn him; this supplies the intended fire-on-flesh action that God's command in 21:69 reverses.
Livestock provide warmth and other benefits and are also eaten from, placing protection from cold beside the animal food behind the section's heated meat and milk dishes.
Abraham goes quietly to his household and returns with a fat calf, opening the parallel meal scene to the roasted calf of 11:69.
He places the calf before his guests and asks why they do not eat, making the cooked animal an offered table rather than merely an object.
God subjects livestock to people so that some carry them and some are eaten, another direct animal-food counterpart to the source-section qaliyya.
Livestock also yield benefits and drinks, joining the milk side of the source-section qahīra to the meat eaten in 36:72.
God made livestock so that people ride some and eat from some; the eating of large livestock directly recalls the source-section camel-meat dish.
Boiling water is poured over the condemned person's head, continuing 44:43-46's meal that boils inside the belly with an external cooking-like action upon the body.
Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring his family a burning brand so that they may warm themselves, presenting fire as useful bodily warmth rather than bodily destruction.
This repeated scene has Moses sight fire and seek a firebrand so that his family may warm themselves, directly connecting seen fire with relief from cold.
Adam and his wife eat from the tree and their nakedness appears; this enacts the loss of the food-and-clothing security promised in 20:118 after the enemy warning of 20:117.
When orphans and needy people attend an estate division, the heirs are told to provide for them from it and speak kindly, joining material nourishment to non-oppressive treatment.
The garden owners go out early determined and believing themselves able to bar others, turning the morning harvest into a deliberate act of deprivation against the poor named in 68:24.
The command to burn the offender in Hell belongs to the same indictment that says in 69:34 he did not urge feeding the poor, joining punitive fire to a withheld meal.
The promise to cast the offender into Saqar supplies the fire destination whose later confession includes failure to feed the poor in 74:44.
The people consume inheritance with voracious consumption immediately after neglecting the orphan and poor, contrasting self-directed devouring with withheld nourishment.
The warning of a blazing fire establishes the fire from which the charitable giver of 92:18 is kept away in 92:17.
Abraham's people build a structure and cast him into the blazing fire, another concrete attempt to let fire take a human body that divine rescue defeats.
The condemned are dragged through boiling water and then burned in the Fire, directly staging heated liquid followed by fire acting upon bodies.
The guilty circulate between Hell and intensely boiling water, binding fire and boiling liquid in the same punitive scene as the section's hot-food senses.
Garments of pitch and fire covering faces give another precise bodily surface upon which fire acts, close to the section's fire-seizing-flesh expression.
The trench is identified as a fire abundantly supplied with fuel in the passage about believers subjected to it, giving the fire-on-human-flesh image a deliberate human setting.
After the command to eat camel meat and feed others, this ayah states that neither flesh nor blood reaches God but piety does, fixing the meal's ethical purpose rather than its cooking alone.
Because of the conduct exemplified by feeding the vulnerable in 76:8, God protects the righteous from the day's evil; 76:13 then specifies their Garden freedom from sun and bitter cold.
Adam and his wife are told to dwell in the Garden and eat freely and plentifully, an indirect parallel to the no-hunger security recalled in the section through 20:118.
Eating from the forbidden tree makes Adam and his wife's nakedness appear, paralleling the food-and-exposure consequences that 20:117-119 frame as loss of Garden security.
The command concerning orphans says reform is best and, if households are mixed, the orphans are brothers; it replaces dominating isolation with protected shared life.
The command to stand for justice for orphans supplies the positive social relation opposite the qahr forbidden toward the orphan in the section.
Approaching orphan property is barred except in the best manner until maturity, giving a concrete boundary against overpowering the vulnerable orphan.
This repeated prohibition protects orphan property until maturity and requires fulfillment of covenant, another specific limit on the human power named by qahr.
The day is sworn by as it displays the sun, continuing 91:1's sun and its ḍuḥā with the full daylight manifestation of that brightness.
The night covers the sun after the day displays it, paralleling the forenoon-and-stilled-night pair that opens surah 93.
The people exchange manna and quails for a list of ordinary plant foods, and humiliation and poverty follow; the ayah makes choice of food and a state of deprivation part of one scene.
The inhabitant of Hell is given foul fluid to drink, turning served provision into bodily harm rather than relief from thirst.
He tries to gulp the drink but can scarcely swallow it, and death comes from every side without ending him; this completes the anti-nourishing drink scene of 14:16.
In the greatest fire the condemned person neither dies nor lives, making heat suspend the ordinary boundary of bodily life rather than simply cooking or consuming flesh.
God brings forth green pasture, supplying the living green vegetation that the source-section qily definition says is burned; the ayah itself does not mention burning.
The pasture becomes dark stubble, resembling the dark residue of the source-section plant ash, though this ayah does not identify the process as fire.
Rain-fed vegetation becomes dry debris scattered by wind, an indirect parallel to the source-section wet plants becoming ash and to Quranic windblown ash; the ayah contains no fire.
Water produces varied crops that then yellow and become broken residue, a repeated plant-to-residue transformation related indirectly to the source-section qily ash, without explicit burning.
Vegetation delights its growers, then yellows and becomes debris; it offers another indirect living-plant-to-residue parallel, but no fire or ash is named.

The Fire's fuel is people and stones, bringing heated stone and human flesh together as the source-section qahīra and qahr senses separately do; the culinary bridge is indirect because the stones here are fuel.
A Fire fueled by people and stones repeats the conjunction of bodies, fire, and stone behind the source-section hot-stone and fire-on-flesh images, though no meal is present.

The prisoner's dream of carrying bread from which birds eat preserves flour transformed into food, indirectly recalling the flour added to the source-section qahīra; the ayah names bread rather than flour or heat.
